evidence.clarity: 1440 and 390: the H1 'Nobody asks "is it out yet?"' names the outcome. evidence.fit: The member path is strong: the hero sample kiln is the member's view, and a 'For members' block plus the footer line 'Members: ask your studio for an invite' cover joining. The owner path is thin, though the brief says the owner pays and must trust the page with their schedule. evidence.distinctiveness: The kiln cross-section has shelves, element coils and pots stamped with chop-mark initials (MR, JO, AK), set on a clay-red band with typewriter-style 'Sample...' labels. The door sheet ('who took my spot??') sits beside a before/after table. You would recognise this as a pottery product with the logo removed. The later sections (comparison table, log table, CTA band) follow a more standard pattern.
evidence.proof: 1440: the whole core job is operable in the first screen: claim a spot, step through Loading/Firing/Cooling/Out, see the message. The counts agree everywhere (7 of 12 claimed, 8 after my claim, 'you and the 7 other members'), and the log row 'Thursday bisque, Loading, 7 of 12 claimed' matches the hero. evidence.first_screen: 1440 and 390: one viewport holds a specific outcome (nobody asks 'is it out yet?'), the named audience (community pottery studios, owners vs members), an operable labelled sample kiln that makes the promise believable, and a CTA whose label and note match what the brief's URL offers.

problems: Owner path is thin for the person who pays: one paragraph and a log table, with nothing showing the owner sets firings, limits shelf space or controls the stage. That is the brief's 'trust it with their schedule' tension.
Nothing says what happens after 'Start your free 30-day trial' (what setup involves, or how members get invited once the owner is in).
Later sections repeat the hero's idea (before/after table, closing 'Take the sign-up sheet off the kiln room door'), spending space that could have gone to the owner.

reason: As an owner arriving cold on a laptop and as a member on a phone, B tells me in one line what it is and who it is for, and lets me run the whole job (claim, follow the firing, get the message) in the first screen with consistent, clearly labelled sample numbers. A answers the owner's trust question better but implies a kiln-temperature feed the brief never mentions and its examples contradict each other. A clearly built-out owner-control section on B would make the choice easy. If the owner's schedule-trust were the deciding test, A's owner section could flip it.
